title: New Zealand Signed a Trade Deal With India. Then It Quietly Started Writing Immigration Rules That Apply to Indians — and Only Indians.
excerpt: Even NZ's own Foreign Minister calls the proposed restrictions discriminatory. Days before Modi's first-ever visit, the country's coalition government is tearing itself apart over who gets to come in.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • New Zealand's new immigration rules target Indian nationals exclusively, raising accusations of discrimination.
  • Foreign Minister Peters warns that these restrictions could harm New Zealand's international reputation.
  • The India-New Zealand FTA allows 5,000 Indian professionals to work in New Zealand, contradicting new immigration rules.
  • Anti-Indian sentiment is rising in New Zealand, fueled by political rhetoric and protests.
  • Prime Minister Modi's upcoming visit is overshadowed by immigration controversies despite the new trade agreement.
Peters and NZ First oppose the deal outright, arguing it gives too much away on immigration without sufficient reciprocity on dairy market access. "National preferred doing a quick, low-quality deal over doing the hard work necessary to get a fair deal that delivers for both New Zealanders and Indians," he said. NZ First has invoked the coalition's "agree to disagree" provision and will vote against the enabling legislation. The National Party, which leads the coalition, has secured opposition Labour Party support to push the ratification through Parliament. But the simultaneous move to restrict Indian immigration through separate policy settings — even as the FTA promises mobility — strikes many observers as contradictory at best and bad faith at worst. ## A Community Under Pressure For New Zealand's approximately 250,000-strong Indian diaspora, the developments arrive amid a wider chill. Anti-immigration sentiment has sharpened across the country in recent years, driven by housing pressure, high youth unemployment, and stretched public services. Far-right figures, including Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki, have staged protests explicitly targeting Indian immigration, holding signs reading "enough is enough" and calling for a freeze on arrivals from India. The movement, while fringe, has grown more visible as the FTA debate has intensified. The New Zealand government also launched a separate probe into the exploitation of migrant workers from India and Bangladesh — a real and documented problem in sectors like construction, agriculture, and hospitality. But community leaders worry that the exploitation narrative is being weaponised to restrict all Indian migration, rather than to protect the workers themselves. "There are NZ citizens of Indian race who will face the brunt of this racism," one social media user wrote in a widely shared response to Jones' comments. "Normalising usage of racist slurs like 'butter chicken' is criminal."

## Timing Is Everything The internal NZ fight lands at an acutely sensitive moment. Modi is expected in New Zealand in the second week of July — the first visit by an Indian Prime Minister in over 40 years. The visit was meant to celebrate the FTA as a milestone in bilateral ties. Instead, it will unfold against the backdrop of a government that signed a trade deal with India while simultaneously writing immigration rules designed to keep Indians out.

India's government has so far been measured in its public response, with the Ministry of External Affairs noting the importance of the bilateral relationship without directly addressing the immigration controversy. But diplomatic sources suggest New Delhi is watching closely, particularly given the India-specific nature of the proposed restrictions.For NRIs in New Zealand, the message is unsettling: the same government that welcomed Indian trade is not sure it wants Indian people. How Modi navigates this contradiction — publicly or privately — may define whether the FTA delivers on its promise or becomes a symbol of how economic partnerships can coexist with targeted exclusion. *Sources: Bloomberg via Hindu Business Line, Reuters, BBC World Service, New Zealand Parliament (Hansard), NZ First Party, Dainik Jagran, Inshorts, VisaVerge*
